createOrReplace.title: India Manufacturing PMI Hits 9-Month High of 56.0
createOrReplace.html:
India manufacturing PMI rose to a nine-month high of 56.0 in November 2026, up from 54.7 in October, according to the HSBC Flash India PMI reported by Business Standard. Factory output, new orders, hiring and purchasing all picked up, while services growth eased to 55.3. The composite index edged up to 56.3, so private-sector growth is steady, with factories now doing the lifting.

This matters now because the flash reading lands a week before the final numbers, due on 1 December for manufacturing and 3 December for services, and just as plants plan Q4 production and pre-budget inventory. It also comes after a soft patch in hard data: official industrial production growth slowed to 6.7% in September. For founders and operations heads, the question is whether November's pickup is real demand or stock-building, and what to do with the window either way.

TL;DR

  • The HSBC flash India manufacturing PMI hit 56.0 in November 2026, a nine-month high, against a consensus of 54.5 reported by Trading Economics.
  • The manufacturing output index rose to 58.3 from 57.0, while services activity slipped to 55.3 from 55.8.
  • The composite PMI was 56.3, its 64th consecutive month above the 50 line, and the highest since June's 57.1.
  • Official IIP growth slowed to 6.7% in September from a revised 7.8% in August, though manufacturing still grew 7.6%.
  • Capital goods output grew 10.4% and intermediate goods 12.2% in September, so investment demand has not stalled.

What did the November 2026 flash PMI show?

It showed factories accelerating and services cooling: the flash manufacturing PMI rose to 56.0, services activity fell to 55.3, and the composite edged up to 56.3.

Business Standard reports that the HSBC Flash India Manufacturing PMI climbed from 54.7 in October, while the manufacturing output index rose to 58.3 from 57.0. Total new business grew at the fastest pace since June, and new export orders rose at the quickest rate in four months. Any reading above 50 means expansion, and the composite has now stayed above that line for 64 straight months, according to a second Business Standard report.

The services side was softer. The services business activity index slipped to 55.3 from 55.8, and service providers cut headcount for the first time in close to a year. S&P Global's survey summary, quoted by Business Standard, said quicker factory growth largely offset the softer services increase. ETV Bharat, carrying the IANS report, also notes that year-ahead sentiment was the best since May.

Why did the India manufacturing PMI jump in November?

Because output, new orders, hiring and purchasing all accelerated at once, and firms built inventory at a record pace.

Trading Economics, which tracks the S&P Global series, reports that manufacturers hired at the strongest rate in seven months and bought inputs at the fastest pace since May. Stocks of purchases rose at the quickest rate in nine months. The striking detail is finished goods: Business Standard reports holdings rose by the greatest extent since the survey began in March 2005.

That last number cuts both ways. Firms may be stocking up ahead of expected orders, which is a confident signal. Or output is running ahead of sales, which becomes a problem if demand cools in Q4. Margins also helped. HSBC's chief India economist Pranjul Bhandari said, as quoted by Business Standard, that "input-cost inflation stayed subdued, while output-price inflation increased modestly supporting margins".

How does 56.0 compare with recent months?

It is the best reading since February 2026 and well above the long-run average, though still short of the August 2025 record.

Trading Economics shows the manufacturing PMI at 55.1 in September and 54.7 in October, the latter revised down from a preliminary 54.9. November's 56.0 reverses that two-month drift. For context, the series has averaged 53.46 since 2012 and peaked at an all-time high of 59.30 in August 2025. So November is a good month, not an extraordinary one.

One caution on method. The flash estimate is based on around 90% of monthly survey responses, Business Standard notes, and the final reading can move. October's own revision from 54.9 to 54.7 is a reminder that a tenth or two either way is normal.

Does official industrial production data back up the PMI?

Partly: IIP growth slowed to 6.7% in September, but manufacturing still grew 7.6% and capital goods 10.4%, so the hard data show slower but solid growth.

According to DD News, citing the government's quick estimates, September IIP growth eased from a revised 7.8% in August, down from the earlier quick estimate of 8%. ThePrint reports the year's peak came in June at 8.8%, while News On AIR reported July revised up to 7.4%. Cumulative growth for April–September 2026 was 6.8%, against 4.4% a year earlier, ThePrint found, so the first half of FY27 is well ahead of last year.

Manufacturing, which carries a 76.06% weight in the index, grew 7.6% in September after a revised 8.6% in August, and 7.5% for April–September, DD News reports. Electricity and gas supply grew 11.2%, while mining contracted 6.2%. Seventeen of 23 manufacturing industry groups grew. Electrical equipment rose 33.9%, motor vehicles 19% and beverages 39.4%, while pharmaceuticals contracted 8.9%. The September numbers are quick estimates compiled at an 86.5% weighted response rate, so they will be revised too.

What should manufacturers do with this PMI signal?

Treat it as a planning input, not a forecast: check whether your own order book matches the survey, then tighten inventory and capacity decisions before Q4.

  1. Compare the PMI with your own data. If your new orders are not rising like the survey's, you are losing share or sit in a weaker segment. Pull order intake by product family and region for the last 12 weeks.
  2. Watch finished-goods stock. The survey's record finished-goods build is a warning for anyone carrying stock without firm orders. Set days-of-cover limits per SKU and review them weekly, not monthly.
  3. Lock in input prices while costs are subdued. With input-cost inflation subdued and output prices rising modestly, this is a window to renegotiate annual supply contracts.
  4. Plan hiring in shifts, not headcount. Hiring hit a seven-month high. Use contract and overtime capacity first until the final December readings and October IIP data, due 30 November, confirm the trend.
  5. Automate the tracking. Put PMI, IIP and your own plant data on one weekly dashboard so the comparison takes minutes, not a meeting.

This is where demand forecasting and inventory tools earn their keep. A model that blends your order history with external signals such as PMI new orders and IIP category growth will flag a stock build earlier than a monthly spreadsheet review.

What this means for Indian businesses

For Indian manufacturers, November's data say demand is holding up and margins have room, but the inventory build needs watching. Capital goods growth of 10.4% in September and intermediate goods at 12.2% suggest that other firms are still investing in capacity. Consumer non-durables at 1.4% say rural and mass consumption is not yet carrying its share.

Firms supplying machinery, electrical equipment and auto components have the strongest tailwind, given 33.9% growth in electrical equipment and 19% in motor vehicles in September. Pharma exporters face the opposite picture. Frequently asked questions

What is the India manufacturing PMI?

The India manufacturing PMI is a monthly survey index of purchasing managers at Indian factories, compiled by S&P Global and sponsored by HSBC. It combines new orders, output, employment, supplier delivery times and stocks of purchases. A reading above 50 means activity expanded from the previous month; below 50 means it contracted. A flash estimate comes out late in the month, followed by a final reading early the next month.

What was India's manufacturing PMI in November 2026?

The HSBC Flash India Manufacturing PMI was 56.0 in November 2026, up from 54.7 in October and a nine-month high, according to Business Standard. The flash composite PMI was 56.3 and the services activity index was 55.3. The final manufacturing reading is due on 1 December and the final services reading on 3 December 2026.

Is the flash PMI the same as the final PMI?

No. The flash PMI is an early estimate based on around 90% of monthly survey responses, so the final reading can differ slightly. In October 2026, for example, the preliminary manufacturing reading of 54.9 was revised to a final 54.7, according to Trading Economics. Revisions of one or two tenths are common and rarely change the direction of the signal.

How is the PMI different from the IIP?

The PMI is a survey of whether activity rose or fell compared with the previous month, released within weeks. The IIP is the government's measure of actual industrial output against the same month a year earlier, released about four weeks after the month ends. In September 2026 the IIP grew 6.7% year on year, while the PMI showed continued but slower expansion.

Why does a high finished-goods inventory reading matter?

Finished-goods stock rose at the fastest pace since the survey began in March 2005, according to Business Standard. That can mean firms expect strong orders, or that production is outrunning sales. If demand softens, excess stock ties up working capital and forces discounting, so manufacturers should check days of cover by product before adding more output.
